items.title: STAX Framework
items.text:
A modern open-source opinionated GitHub Workflow Framework to combine and deploy all of your cloud infrastructure and services.

Developed by GEBIT Solutions.

Get started → Explore supported technologies →

items.title: Backends
items.text: stax owns the Terraform/OpenTofu backend type: the pipeline writes an override file with an azurerm backend for cloud: azure, an s3 backend for cloud: aws, or a local backend for stacks with local_backend: true. Keep an empty backend "s3" {} (or backend "azurerm" {}) block in the stack, or none at all; the bucket, key, region and flags come from the deployment context.

items.title: AWS S3
items.text: For cloud: aws the state lives in state_bucket_name in state_region, one key per stack. State is locked with S3 native locking (use_lockfile), which needs OpenTofu 1.10 or Terraform 1.11 or later. Create the bucket with the setup-state workflow (cloud: aws); it enables versioning, default encryption, a public access block, a TLS-only bucket policy and managed tags. Pass dry_run: true to only check the bucket and list what would change.

items.title: S3-compatible storage
items.text:
The S3 backend also works with S3-compatible stores such as Wasabi or MinIO. Point stax at the store with the optional deployment fields (or their GitHub variables):

deployment:
  cloud: aws
  default_location: eu-central-2
  state_region: eu-central-2
  state_bucket_name: example-tfstate
  aws_endpoint_url_s3: https://s3.eu-central-2.wasabisys.com
  aws_endpoint_url_sts: https://sts.wasabisys.com
  aws_endpoint_url_iam: https://iam.wasabisys.com
  aws_s3_compatible: true
  state_use_lockfile: false   # only until the store is known to support conditional writes
Field Effect aws_endpoint_url, aws_endpoint_url_s3, aws_endpoint_url_sts, aws_endpoint_url_iam Exported as AWS_ENDPOINT_URL, AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3, … to the init, plan, apply and output steps and the STS identity check. The S3 backend, the AWS provider and the AWS CLI read them. Other job steps, such as the SSM keystore, keep using AWS. aws_s3_compatible: true Sets AWS_REQUEST_CHECKSUM_CALCULATION and AWS_RESPONSE_CHECKSUM_VALIDATION to when_required for those steps and adds skip_s3_checksum, skip_region_validation and skip_requesting_account_id to the backend. aws_skip_sts_check: true Skips aws sts get-caller-identity and adds skip_credentials_validation to the backend. Use it for stores without an STS endpoint. state_use_lockfile: false Turns off S3 native locking for stores that do not support conditional writes. Nothing stops two runs of a stack from writing the state at the same time, so serialize deployments yourself. state_use_path_style: true Uses path-style addressing (https://host/bucket/key), which MinIO usually needs.

Notes:

  • Authenticate with the static AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY secrets. GitHub OIDC exchanges its token at AWS STS, so OIDC_ENABLED cannot be combined with aws_endpoint_url or aws_endpoint_url_sts.
  • The provider in your stack still needs settings that the backend flags do not cover, for example skip_region_validation and skip_requesting_account_id in the aws provider block for non-AWS regions.
  • For the state bucket, call the setup-state workflow with the same endpoints and aws_s3_compatible: "true". Versioning is required; public access block, default encryption, the TLS-only policy and tagging only warn when the store does not support them.

items.title: Deployment context
items.text:
Put deployment values under the top-level deployment mapping in configs/<name>.yaml, or set them as GitHub variables. The setup workflow reads this mapping to build the deployment environment. stax init lists every required value, each next to its GitHub variable, in one commented deployment block of configs/default.yaml. stax init --project shop additionally writes deployment.project: shop live.

# configs/default.yaml
deployment:
  project: shop
  customer_id: default
  stage: dev
  cloud: azure
  default_location: northeurope
  public_cloud_flag: true
  resource_group_name: rg-shop-dev
  dns_zone_name: example.com
  dns_zone_resource_group_name: rg-dns
  state_storage_account_name: shopstate
  state_container_name: shop-tfstate
  state_resource_group_name: rg-state
stacks: []

# configs/prod.yaml
deployment:
  stage: prod
  resource_group_name: rg-shop-prod
  state_container_name: shop-prod-tfstate
stacks: []

Selecting configs/prod.yaml uses its stage, resource group and state container. Supply the remaining required values through GitHub variables or add them to that selected YAML. Add a stack to the selected file before deploying; setup rejects an empty stack list.

The setup workflow reads only the files you select. configs/default.yaml is a normal config file: it contributes no values when you select prod. The same rule applies to external configuration repositories.

For multiple configs, pass release_config_filepath: configs/prod.yaml,configs/region.yaml to the setup reusable workflow. Later selected files override earlier values in the shared run context. The generated Deploy form selects one config by name.

Precedence per field is selected YAML → GitHub variable. An empty string or null falls through to the GitHub variable if no other selected file supplies the field; false remains an explicit value.

items.title: Supported fields and GitHub variable fallback
items.text:
YAML deployment field GitHub variable Requirement project PROJECT (vars.project also works) Required customer_id CUSTOMER_ID Required stage STAGE Required cloud CLOUD Required; azure or aws default_location DEFAULT_LOCATION Required public_cloud_flag PUBLIC_CLOUD_FLAG Required; boolean true/false or their string forms resource_group_name RESOURCE_GROUP_NAME Required for Azure dns_zone_name DNS_ZONE_NAME Required for Azure dns_zone_resource_group_name DNS_ZONE_RESOURCE_GROUP_NAME Required for Azure state_storage_account_name STATE_STORAGE_ACCOUNT_NAME Required for Azure state_container_name STATE_CONTAINER_NAME Required for Azure state_resource_group_name STATE_RESOURCE_GROUP_NAME Required for Azure state_bucket_name STATE_BUCKET_NAME Required for AWS state_region STATE_REGION Required for AWS aws_endpoint_url AWS_ENDPOINT_URL Optional, AWS only; base endpoint for every AWS service aws_endpoint_url_s3 AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3 Optional, AWS only; S3 endpoint for the state backend and the AWS provider aws_endpoint_url_sts AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_STS Optional, AWS only; not supported with OIDC_ENABLED aws_endpoint_url_iam AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_IAM Optional, AWS only aws_s3_compatible AWS_S3_COMPATIBLE Optional, AWS only; boolean, default false aws_skip_sts_check AWS_SKIP_STS_CHECK Optional, AWS only; boolean, default false state_use_lockfile STATE_USE_LOCKFILE Optional, AWS only; boolean, default true state_use_path_style STATE_USE_PATH_STYLE Optional, AWS only; boolean, default false

The optional AWS fields target S3-compatible storage such as Wasabi or MinIO; see Backends. Endpoint URLs must use https (http only for localhost, 127.0.0.1 or [::1]) and cannot contain credentials, query strings, fragments, whitespace or backslashes. Setting one of them to a non-default value with another cloud fails the setup.

items.title: Stack conditions
items.text:
A stack's if string is evaluated whether or not a stack filter is supplied. For example, if: "'{stage}' === 'prod'" selects the stack only for the production stage. A false condition excludes the stack; if every selected stack is excluded, the deployment plan is empty.

Previously, unfiltered deployments ignored these conditions. Review existing conditions before upgrading: stacks that previously ran despite a false condition will now be skipped.

items.title: Installation
items.text: Use the STAX CLI to create a deployment workflow, add stacks and validate your configuration. You run the CLI locally; GitHub Actions runs your deployments.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• Node.js 24 or later, with npm.
  • A GitHub repository with GitHub Actions enabled.

Check your local installation:

node --version
npm --version

You do not need cloud credentials to install the CLI or generate project files. Configure credentials and deployment settings before running a deployment.

items.title: Choose an installation method
items.text: Use a project-local installation to share a locked CLI version with your team. Use a global installation to run stax across repositories without adding a dependency to each project. Prefer project-local installation when dealing with multiple projects to avoid version conflicts.

items.title: Project-local installation
items.text:
From the root of your project repository, install the CLI as a development dependency:

npm install --save-dev --save-exact @gebit/stax-cli

If your repository has no package.json yet, create one with npm init -y first.

npm saves the current release as an exact development dependency in your package.json. Add a stax entry to its scripts section, keeping your existing scripts and dependencies:

{
  "scripts": {
    "stax": "stax"
  }
}

Check that you can run the installed CLI:

npm run stax -- --help

Commit package.json and package-lock.json. Add node_modules/ to .gitignore. After cloning the repository, team members install the locked dependencies with:

npm ci

Use npm run stax -- <command> for this installation. npm uses the project's installed CLI; you do not need a global installation.

items.title: Global installation
items.text:
Install the CLI for use across repositories:

npm install --global @gebit/stax-cli

Check that the command is available:

stax --help

Use stax <command> for this installation.

items.title: Initialize your repository
items.text:
From the root of your project repository, run the command for your installation method:

Action Project-local Global Initialize the repository npm run stax -- init stax init Add a stack npm run stax -- add stax add Validate configuration npm run stax -- validate config stax validate config

Both installation methods use the installed CLI version when init writes the reusable workflow refs, actions-version inputs and editor schema URL. Choose a CLI release that matches the framework version you deploy. Existing workflows and configs do not update when you install a different CLI version.

The init command creates two files:

File Purpose .github/workflows/deploy.yml A manually triggered Deploy workflow that calls the STAX reusable workflows. configs/default.yaml An empty stack list, deployment-setting examples and a schema link for editor completion.

If you build the CLI from source (0.0.0-development), pass --framework-ref <tag-or-commit-sha> to init, for example stax init --framework-ref main. You can name a branch, including main, if you want that ref. Development builds have no default framework ref; published releases reject the override and use their installed version.

You can also set a project name and preselect a GitHub Environment during initialization:

# Project-local installation
npm run stax -- init --project my-project --environment dev

# Global installation
stax init --project my-project --environment dev

Use lowercase letters, digits and hyphens for the project name, starting with a letter. Create the GitHub Environment in your repository settings before deploying; --environment only sets the workflow form's default.

STAX leaves existing files unchanged unless you pass --force. Review those files before replacing them.

items.title: Check your configuration
items.text:
Run the validation command for your installation method from the table above. The initial configuration contains no stacks, so the validator reports a warning.

Local validation checks the configuration structure; it does not verify cloud access or guarantee that a deployment will succeed. The CLI allows deployment fields to remain unset because GitHub variables can supply them at runtime.

stax add and stax validate config use the schema bundled with the installed CLI and work offline. They do not fetch the editor schema URL in configs/default.yaml.

stax init does not deploy anything. Before running the generated workflow, add a stack and supply the required deployment settings and credentials. See Configuration for deployment fields and their matching GitHub variables.

items.title: Supported stack types
items.text:
Combine these technologies and workflow types in your STAX Framework deployment stacks.

Checked boxes indicate support. Unchecked boxes indicate planned support, not available yet.

items.title: Infrastructure as code
items.text:
• Terraform (terraform): provision cloud infrastructure.
  • OpenTofu (opentofu): provision cloud infrastructure.
  • Bicep (bicep): provision Azure infrastructure.
  • CDK: planned, not supported yet.

items.title: Docker and image builds
items.text:
• Docker (docker-build-push): build container images and push them to a registry.
  • Packer (packer): build machine images.

items.title: Packages
items.text: • RPM (rpmbuild): build RPM packages.

items.title: Deployments
items.text:
• Cloud functions (function-build-deploy): build and deploy cloud functions.
  • Azure Static Web Apps (swa-site-deploy): deploy websites.
  • Azure Static Web Apps documentation (swa-docs-site-deploy): deploy documentation sites.
  • Amazon S3 (s3-site-deploy): deploy static websites.
  • GitHub Pages (github-pages-site-deploy): build MkDocs or Zensical documentation, or publish a prebuilt static site.

items.title: Scripts
items.text:
Use the script workflow type to run custom scripts:

  • Bash: run shell scripts.
  • Python: run Python scripts.

items.title: Helm deployments
items.text: • Helm: deploy Helm charts to Kubernetes clusters.

items.title: Raw Kubernetes manifest deployments
items.text: • Kubernetes manifests: deploy Kubernetes resources from raw YAML manifests.

items.title: Why STAX?
items.text:
Cloud engineering and DevOps teams solve many of the same CI/CD problems in every project: deploying infrastructure and services, generating releases, reviewing pull requests, running dry runs, and performing static code analysis. Rebuilding these workflows takes time. Keeping copied implementations in sync adds ongoing maintenance work.

Reusable GitHub Actions workflows and actions help reduce that duplication, but they still need project-specific integration. Teams must connect build and deployment steps, configure cloud authentication, manage access to external repositories, and coordinate the order in which components are deployed.

STAX aims to address these challenges by reducing repetitive setup and project-specific integration work. It goes beyond workflow reuse by letting teams describe infrastructure components and their relations in configuration files, making delivery easier to manage as projects grow.

items.title: Bring related components together
items.text:
A project rarely consists of a single deployment. It may combine infrastructure, container images, application builds, scripts, and Kubernetes deployments using manifests or Helm charts.

STAX organizes these units as stacks. The goal is to keep infrastructure provisioning and service delivery together, with a shared approach to configuration and orchestration across different technologies.

items.title: Make dependencies explicit
items.text:
Stacks often depend on one another. A cluster needs its network before it can be provisioned. A container deployment needs both a built image and a running target environment. Some stacks also need output values from earlier deployments, such as a resource identifier or service endpoint.

STAX aims to make these relationships explicit, so deployment order and the flow of values between stacks are part of the project configuration instead of custom coordination logic scattered across workflows.

items.title: Start new projects with less setup
items.text: A consistent framework reduces the decisions and repetitive work involved in getting a project started. STAX aims to help teams bootstrap new projects, reuse deployment patterns, and extend their configuration as new components are added.

items.title: Stay within GitHub
items.text:
STAX draws inspiration from Spacelift and Atmos, particularly their approaches to organizing infrastructure and coordinating stacks.

Its design goal is to provide that orchestration within GitHub Actions, without requiring a separate SaaS platform. Beyond GitHub and the services being deployed, a cloud storage service may be needed to hold values passed between stacks. This orchestration state is distinct from any infrastructure state managed by the underlying tools.
